transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-14 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Samir Rao (Redwood SE), Jo Chen (Redwood SRE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood Solutions), Daniel Kim (Argos ML Platform Lead), Priya Shah (Argos Head Eng), Tom Alvarez (Argos On-prem Ops), Elena Rossi (Argos Security), Speaker 6

Auto-summary (auto): Discussed kernel choices and where TRT-LLM had advantages for dense transformer blocks but vLLM had stronger preemption for low-latency single-stream requests; CUDA Graphs speed up stable paths but can show tail jitter with eviction/prefetch; quantization helps cost but introduces subtle output deviance—need eval sets. Agreed pilot.

[00:00] Maya Patel: ok hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call, we have the Argos team, thanks for making time. um Samir and Jo from our side will drive the kernel and infra bits.
[00:28] Daniel Kim: hey thanks. we're particularly interested in the stability story — we've been seeing some flakiness with our current TRT setup when we try to keep persistent KV caches across long conversations.
[01:05] Samir Rao: cool yeah that's exactly what we wanted to dig into. to frame the convo, we'll compare two main exec paths: TRT-LLM optimized kernels and the vLLM async execution path. we'll also look at CUDA Graphs interactions and quantization choices.
[01:42] Priya Shah: and we want the on-prem angle — Argos needs VPC-like isolation, HSM-backed keys, and we need to validate throughput for our 2xA100 racks.
[02:10] Jo Chen: quick clarifying q: when you say "flakiness" — is that OOMs, or timeouts, or correctness divergence?
[02:25] Daniel Kim: mostly timeouts and sometimes a blank token stream mid-generation; it seems correlated to long sequence lengths (1.5k+ tokens) and a mix of small bursts and a few long-running sessions.
[02:48] Samir Rao: that matches a known edge: CUDA Graphs provide big perf wins when the kernel graph is stable, but when you have eviction/prefetch behavior for KV cache and the kernel selection changes mid-stream, the graph needs to be rebuilt which can cause spikes.
[03:20] Tom Alvarez: do we have a simple reproducer? we can try to run something in our lab.
[03:33] Samir Rao: yes — we asked Argos to share a prompt set and seq distribution. Daniel will drop that. We'll run a kernel sweep across model sizes to see where TRT-LLM gives net wins vs vLLM.
[04:05] Maya Patel: also note cost tradeoffs: TRT-LLM tends to beat in raw tokens/sec for dense batched workloads, but vLLM's preemption reduces tail latency for single request workloads.
[04:31] Elena Rossi: security question — if we're doing on-prem, how do we integrate KMS? we are not sharing keys.
[04:45] Jo Chen: for on-prem we support customer-managed KMS/HSM endpoints; Redwood's control plane can be air-gapped, and Jo will share the integration notes.
[05:03] Speaker 6: (inaudible) question about, um, quantization—does 4-bit cause hallucination jumps?
[05:20] Samir Rao: short answer: sometimes. 4-bit (particularly aggressive QLoRA-style or recent group-wise schemes) can change logits enough to affect decoding in narrow prompts. but if you employ mixed-precision fallback for attention or final layers, you can keep most fidelity while still getting ~1.8-2.4x perf improvements.
[05:56] Daniel Kim: our team is evaluating 13B and 70B models; 70B is our target for higher-quality tasks. anything different there?
[06:12] Samir Rao: 70B is more sensitive. quantization and kernel path selection both matter more as model size scales — kernel tiling choices, attention kernel numerics, and whether the runtime uses fused kernels (TRT) vs more flexible vLLM op-by-op execution. We'll include 7B/13B/70B in the sweep.
[06:43] Priya Shah: can you explain the eviction/prefetch interaction with CUDA Graphs? I've seen the term but not the mechanics.
[06:59] Jo Chen: sure — so CUDA Graphs capture a fixed sequence of GPU ops. with persistent KV cache we avoid recomputing keys/values but eviction introduces memory moves and when the runtime decides to evict or prefetch KV segments (NUMA-aware or multi-GPU sharding), the op sequence changes. that invalidates a recorded graph and forces rebuild or fallback to non-graph path which can be expensive.
[07:45] Tom Alvarez: that explains our spikes. we saw a rebuild at around the 45-second mark of some long sessions.
[07:55] Samir Rao: yes, and more nuance: TRT-LLM's fused kernels often lead to fewer kernel launches (nice for CUDA Graphs), but can be less tolerant to mid-stream changes. vLLM is more dynamic — it has more launches but better opportunistic preemption.
[08:20] Maya Patel: i'd add: the right choice depends on your traffic profile. for mostly batched throughput (e.g., embeddings, bulk generation), TRT wins. for low-latency singletons with bursty traffic, vLLM or a hybrid routing policy can be better.
[08:48] Daniel Kim: hybrid routing sounds interesting — can we route certain routes to vLLM and others to TRT-LLM?
[08:57] Liam Ortiz: yes, we can do policy-based routing by route or token length. we can pin long-session routes to vLLM if you want steadier tail behavior.
[09:18] Priya Shah: about NUMA issues — our racks are 2xA100 per node, NVLink enabled. do we have proven patterns for KV sharding?
[09:30] Jo Chen: we've seen two patterns: per-GPU full model shard with NVLink exchange for KV vs intra-node sharded KV per GPU. NVLink helps but increases cross-GPU synchronization. We'll test both; the bench harness can emulate your topology.
[09:54] Speaker 6: quick interjection — any gotchas with CUDA Graphs and multi-GPU?
[10:05] Samir Rao: yes — graph capture across multiple devices is trickier. Graphs that include NVLink transfers can still be captured, but the timing surface is complex; multi-device graphs are brittle if the sharding changes. So again, predictable op flow helps.
[10:35] Daniel Kim: what about prefetch window sizing? we get OOMs if we prefetch too aggressively.
[10:47] Jo Chen: prefetch window tuning is critical. if you prefetch too far ahead with large seq it floods memory; too conservative and you get stalls. We use a dynamic heuristic based on observed seq lengths and real-time eviction metrics. We'll share the heuristic.
[11:12] Maya Patel: moving to quantization — Samir, can you summarize our recommended profiles for Argos?
[11:20] Samir Rao: for 13B we recommend 4-bit quant with group-wise scales and attention in fp16; that usually yields 1.8-2x perf with small deviance on eval sets. For 70B, we recommend 8-bit or mixed 4/16-bit: keep critical layers in fp16 (attention prox, output layers) and quantize feed-forward parts. We'll also test a calibration pass with your prompts — that helps reduce divergence.
[12:01] Priya Shah: calibration pass — is that expensive? how long?
[12:08] Samir Rao: depends on prompt set size. Usually a few minutes to an hour for a representative 10-1000 prompt set on a 2xA100 node. We'll give you an estimate once you send the data.
[12:25] Elena Rossi: from security — we need to ensure model weights aren't exfiltrated. any risk in quantization/graph capture when kernels are fused and vendor binaries are used?
[12:38] Jo Chen: no, quantization itself doesn't expose weights. fused kernels are binaries but run within the customer's infra for on-prem; Redwood does not need access to raw weights in the private deployment. For hosted deployments we sandbox kernels; for private we'll follow your air-gapped process. We'll share the security docs (SOC 2, certs).
[13:05] Maya Patel: ok let's walk through a proposed pilot plan: two phases — (1) kernel selection sweep in Redwood lab with Argos sample prompts; (2) on-prem bench run with your actual 2xA100 node to validate real network and NVLink behavior.
[13:30] Daniel Kim: timeline?
[13:33] Maya Patel: sweep in next week (we'll return results 2026-05-21), on-prem bench the following week (week of 2026-05-25).
[13:46] Tom Alvarez: For on-prem, what's needed from our side?
[13:50] Jo Chen: access to a non-prod node, SSH + docker runtime, your KMS/HSM endpoints (if integration test), and a firewall rule to allow the bench controller to fetch results (or we can do air-gapped by shipping a USB image).
[14:12] Priya Shah: prefer air-gapped if possible. we don't want outbound rules.
[14:18] Jo Chen: fine — we'll prepare an image you can run locally and a result uploader script you can vet.
[14:28] Samir Rao: back to perf specifics — we'll run latency P50/P95/P99, throughput tokens/sec, and kernel-level counters (SM occupancy, tensor core utilization, kernel launch counts). we'll capture moments where CUDA Graphs reconstruct.
[14:57] Daniel Kim: how do you detect a graph rebuild? can you instrument that?
[15:04] Samir Rao: yes, we'll instrument the runtime hooks; we log graph capture and rebuild events with timestamps and stack traces to correlate with spikes.
[15:20] Speaker 6: oh and can we get memory footprint per layer?
[15:28] Jo Chen: we can approximate per-layer KV cost and request a small tracing build to report real allocations. there's a slight overhead to tracing but ok for bench runs.
[15:44] Priya Shah: about routing — you mentioned policy that splits by route or token length. is that supported in the private deploy?
[15:55] Liam Ortiz: yes, same control plane routing rules apply for private — you can do route-level policies, length thresholds, or user-tier based. The runtime routes to the configured flavor.
[16:12] Daniel Kim: and we can test a canary to send 10% of traffic to TRT and 90% vLLM?
[16:21] Maya Patel: yep — canary and auto-fallback if latency or error rate crosses thresholds.
[16:32] Elena Rossi: on compliance — do you retain logs? we need audit logs and the ability to disable PII capture.
[16:42] Jo Chen: we have configurable retention; for private you control logs and retention. we support redaction hooks.
[16:52] Samir Rao: returning to numerical fidelity — we'll include evaluation metrics (BLEU-ish / ROUGE / task-specific scoring) comparing quant profiles. we recommend you pick 3-5 golden prompts to watch for regressions.
[17:10] Daniel Kim: yes we'll pick about 20 regen prompts across our main tasks.
[17:18] Priya Shah: on the kernel sweep doc — what format will you share results in?
[17:24] Samir Rao: spreadsheet with per-model per-profile rows: model, batch size, seq length, path (TRT-LLM / vLLM / hybrid), tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latencies, graph rebuild count, correctness metric, notes. We'll also attach kernel-level perf counters.
[17:45] Tom Alvarez: if TRT wins for certain sizes, can we pin those routes to dedicated GPUs?
[17:51] Liam Ortiz: yes — you can reserve GPU pools and pin models. Dedicated mode also helps if you want consistent latency SLOs.
[18:03] Maya Patel: we should talk about the cost tradeoff: reserved nodes vs shared. For Argos' scale, reserved 2xA100 per critical route might make sense. We'll include costing estimates in the follow-up.
[18:20] Priya Shah: quick question: are there known cases where quantization + CUDA Graphs interact poorly?
[18:30] Samir Rao: yes — quantization can change kernel shapes (padding, fuse decisions) and therefore the captured graph cache keys. That can cause slightly higher rebuild rates in some aggressive quant profiles. We'll test that explicitly.
[18:49] Daniel Kim: about evaluation — do you have an automated regression alert if quality drops after a rollout?
[18:56] Maya Patel: Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring tied to prompt sets; we can configure regression alerts and auto rollback triggers. We'll demo that in the next call if helpful.
[19:12] Elena Rossi: we need to validate crypto-in-use: HSM key wrapping, TLS mTLS for control plane, and whether model metadata leaves the box.
[19:24] Jo Chen: we'll provide our security package and a private deployment checklist. also note: when private, control plane talks are optional — you can keep everything local.
[19:40] Speaker 6: small nit: how do you handle model updates? we don't want auto-pull without approval.
[19:47] Liam Ortiz: by default private deployments do not auto-pull model changes. you control rollouts and can do A/B.
[19:55] Maya Patel: closing toward logistics — Daniel, you'll send prompt set + seq distribution by 2026-05-19; Redwood runs lab sweep and shares spreadsheet by 2026-05-21; then an on-prem bench week of 2026-05-25. Any blockers?
[20:15] Daniel Kim: timeline looks good. question on instrumentation: can Redwood run bench without outbound connectivity?
[20:22] Jo Chen: yes, image + result uploader script you can run locally; we can also provide an offline sar/trace collection bundle.
[20:38] Priya Shah: for the on-prem run we'd prefer the image approach.
[20:44] Jo Chen: noted. we'll prepare two variants: online and air-gapped.
[20:50] Samir Rao: final technical note: we recommend capturing kernel-level counters and also the sequence state transitions (when KV flips from local to sharded). That will help us correlate rebuilds to logic.
[21:10] Tom Alvarez: do you support collecting NVLink counters?
[21:16] Jo Chen: yes, via nvidia-smi/power & nvlink counters in our tracing harness. there's a small perf overhead but acceptable for acceptance benches.
[21:33] Speaker 6: are there any licensing constraints for TRT-LLM?
[21:39] Maya Patel: TRT-LLM leverages NVIDIA libraries; on private you'll need to accept NVIDIA runtime terms. We'll note that in the follow-up.
[21:52] Daniel Kim: ok thanks.
[21:58] Maya Patel: quick recap: deliverables and owners: Samir kernel sweep (7/13/70B), Jo bench image + harness, Daniel supply prompts + infra access, Elena supply KMS details. We'll include security docs and quotes.
[22:18] Priya Shah: can we schedule a focused 90-min bench kickoff with Tom and our infra team for the on-prem run?
[22:25] Maya Patel: yes, we'll set that up for week of 2026-05-25.
[22:32] Daniel Kim: any open technical concerns we didn't cover?
[22:37] Tom Alvarez: just to emphasize NUMA sharding patterns — please be sure we test both full-shard and per-gpu sharding.
[22:45] Samir Rao: will do.
[22:50] Elena Rossi: and a final ask from security: can we get a short threat model for private deployment? maybe a 1-pager.
[22:58] Jo Chen: yes. we'll provide a 1-pager and the detailed security checklist.
[23:08] Maya Patel: great. thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and scheduling invites.
[23:12] (cross talk)
